purpose: Record of every audio tour segment rendered: spoken text, hashes, duration and request id. Keys are published write-once under audio/.

entries.spokenText: A head drawn as a box, and the box is grinning. This is where the Faces begin, on October 26, 2021, with a white square head on green, two starburst eyes in boxes and a grid of block teeth. Twenty-seven works hang here, nearly all from the five weeks that followed, and every one of them builds a face out of rectangles. They are the happiest works in the collection, and that is not an accident of color. The box head is a toy, and it knows it.

The box is a frame for parts. Eyes go in as rings, spirals or targets, one in each square. The mouth is a second box with teeth set in it like a grille. A nose is a triangle or a bar. Around the parts the box is filled with scribble, hatching or stripes until it is solid, and then the whole thing is set on a flat color. This is a kit, and the pleasure of the room is watching the artist find out how many faces one kit can make. The spirals in the eyes are the tell: a spiral eye is dizzy, not angry, and the grille of teeth under it is a grin.

Watch the boxes tilt. The first heads sit square. By December they lean, stack and turn, and by the following spring the box has become a tall stack with a mouth of giant bars. One head near the end has shadow in its cheeks and spirals in its eyes, and for a moment the toy looks back at you like a person. Then the box grows ears, and it is a toy again.
Four works from the first five weeks, October 26 to November 27, 2021. The box head arrives, loosens, and tilts, and from the first day the mouth is a grin.

The first work in the series. A white box head on green, two eyes as cyan starbursts in square frames, a nose of two yellow bars, and a mouth drawn as a grid of white block teeth. A red zigzag runs along the top like a hairline, and green, yellow and brown lines loop around the whole head. Seventy-seven strokes. Everything the room does is already here: the box, the parts in boxes, the grid of teeth. And the face is pleased with itself, which is where the whole collection starts.
A head in red, green and black scribble with a mane of red marks, one box eye ringed in white, and a wide red mouth at the lower right, open on white teeth, laughing at something off the page.

An angular head in red, blue and yellow line on lavender, with an X in one box eye and bars in the other, a triangle mouth with green zigzag teeth, and a crown of spikes: the first X eye in the collection, and it is a wink.

A head tipped on its side inside a yellow frame, drawn as a dense weave of white, green, orange and magenta lines, with two round eyes and a wide mouth at the bottom, like a picture that fell off the wall and kept smiling.

November 30 and December 1, 2021, eight heads in two days. The parts settle: ringed eyes, triangle noses, boxed teeth. This is the kit being learned, fast, and the faces are delighted with themselves.

Two square eyes side by side, each a red and white target in a box, a red zigzag at the right like a cheek, and below them a long box of white triangle teeth. Cyan hatching runs across the eyes in diagonals. The ground is white with black and green marks at the edges. It is the clearest stack of boxes in the room: eye, eye, mouth, nothing else. The record adds a detail the picture does not show: this one was drawn from a second n n x y z address and sent to the first the same day, and it is still the purest statement of the kit.

A yellow box head on red with a row of white spikes along the top for hair, two ringed eyes with black pupils, a triangle nose, and a box of white teeth under it. Two white hands reach up at the sides, and two small feet stand at the bottom edge. Green, pink and blue hatching fills the box. Nothing else in the room took as many strokes: 801. The hands are up and the feet are planted, and the face in the middle is simply glad to be here. It is the room's self-portrait as a toy.
A box head of purple scribble on yellow, two square eyes with black pupils, a triangle nose, and a white slot of a mouth stitched with black lines, a face holding very still.
A box head in profile on teal, wearing a top hat, with a grin of white teeth, drawn in yellow, green and red hatching: the kit dressed up for an evening out.
A box head on brown with a spiral eye and a box eye, yellow ring earrings at both sides, and a row of white block teeth in a red box, the first dark ground in the room and the grin undimmed.

A box head on maroon with slanted brows and spiral eyes, a red mouth of white fangs, drawn in cyan, white and yellow over dense scribble, the one head in these two days that is trying to look fierce and cannot quite manage it.
A crowned box head in profile on white, facing right, drawn in red, yellow and black line, with a grin of white teeth, a king of nothing in particular.
December 1 to 6, 2021. Nine heads. The box leans, the jaw becomes a drawer, and the stack gets taller. The grounds go dark for the first time, and the grins get wider to match.
A box head on navy drawn in cyan and yellow line, two pink spiral eyes, and a mouth of white blocks in a red box, dizzy and content.

A head on dark brown with two ringed eyes under a pointed brow, and below them a jaw drawn as a drawer: a long box of white triangle teeth, then a second box, then a third, stacked down to the bottom edge. The whole head is filled with green, orange and pink scribble. The jaw here is a stack of its own, the first in the room. The teeth are triangles, which should be a threat, and the stacked drawers under them turn the threat into a chest of toys. This is how the room disarms its own monsters.
A head with spiral eyes, spiral cheeks and a white zigzag crown, a V nose and a mouth of white zigzag, drawn in pink, orange and green line on dark brown, every part of it spinning.
A tall box head on black, two green ring eyes under a pink brow, and an open box of a mouth, drawn in pink, magenta and white scribble, the mouth open as if to say something it has not decided on.
A box head on olive with two pink spiral eyes, a long nose, and a wide white mouth with yellow zigzag inside, drawn in green and blue facets, cut like a gem.
A head drawn like a sign: stacked rectangles outlined in yellow, spiral eyes in boxes, and a box of black zigzag teeth, on dark olive, a face that could hang over a shop door.

A head on blue flattened into bands, drawn in yellow, orange and white line: a band of slit eyes with teeth above them, a band of nose, a wide band of lips, and a chin. The box has become a stack of stripes. Set beside the first head in the room, the parts are the same, eyes, nose, teeth, but every one has been pressed flat and widened. The slit eyes are the first in the room that are not open wide, and the face is the first that is tired. It is the only head here that looks like it has had a long day.
A patterned head on red with two spiral eyes, two rows of gappy white teeth, and yellow and green bars at the sides, grinning through the gaps.
January to March 2022. Six heads, spaced weeks apart, in which the box becomes a tall stack and the teeth grow huge. One of them stops being a toy.

A head of stacked patterned planes, one eye a box with a slot and the other a triangle, a band of huge white teeth across the bottom, in blue, red and yellow: the teeth have grown to fill the whole lower face.

A blocky head on plum, painted in gold and yellow with white scribble over it, two red spiral eyes staring out, and a mouth of clenched white teeth in a dark box. The head has weight: the brow and the cheeks are modelled in light and shadow, and the eyes sit in deep sockets. It is the one head in the room with shadow, and the spirals in its eyes are the room's spirals, drawn into a face that looks back. For one work the toy becomes a person, and the person is afraid. The clenched teeth are the room's grin with the fun gone out of it. Then the series moves on, and the box goes back to being a box.

A tall stack of a head on teal, two round white eyes at the top, a mouth of giant white bars in a brown box, drawn in black, brown and blue, a face that is mostly mouth, bellowing or beaming, and from here it is impossible to say which.

A head on blue with one huge black eye in a white ring, four red capsules for a nose, a grid of white teeth in a red box, and a yellow wavy edge down the right, the eye so large the face is all attention.

A box head with cat ears on teal, hatched in orange, black and yellow, with crossed eyes in boxes, a long nose, and a grin of white teeth in a red mouth. The last work in the room, from March 29, 2022, four months after the yellow box head with the spiky hair. The parts are the same: boxed eyes, a triangle nose, teeth in a box. The box has grown ears. After the stacks and the one frightened head, the room ends on a joke, and the joke is the kit itself: give the box ears and it is a cat, and the cat is grinning.

Look again at the first box head, white on green, with its grid of teeth, and then at the cat-eared box from March. One is a box with parts in it. The other is a box with parts in it and ears. Five months of drawing, and the idea held, because the idea was a game, and the game was still fun.

Faces found in a tangle, and most of them are people. The works in this room are drawn as dense, many-colored scribble, and the face comes out of it: a person with glasses, a man in a hat, a girl in a cap, a screaming head in a halo of white. Twenty-one works, from the second drawing in the series on October 27, 2021, to April 2022. Where the box heads next door are toys, these are likenesses, and the feeling in them is the feeling of recognizing someone.

The scribble is not fill. It is the drawing. Hair, cheeks, beards and backgrounds are all the same looping line in different colors, and the features are the places where the line gets dense or changes color. Glasses are two loops. A mouth is a red knot with white inside it. The method is generous: it lets a face arrive slowly, out of noise, the way a face arrives in a crowd. That is why the first works here feel warm even when they grin with fangs.

Watch how the tangle thins, and how the mood goes with it. In the first weeks the whole square is scribble and the faces are amused, dazed or shouting with pleasure. In February two faces are painted with the tangle only on top, and they are angry. By March the scribble has become hatching, and the faces snarl. The line that found friends in the autumn is, by spring, finding people who have had enough.
Five works from October 27 to November 27, 2021. People with glasses and hats, a face lost in magenta, and the first scream, which is a shout of joy.

A face with rectangular glasses and a fanged grin, drawn entirely in scribble: yellow and red for the hair, green and blue for the cheeks, a red knot for the mouth with white teeth inside it. The glasses are two white loops joined by a bar. The second work in the series, from October 27, 2021. Where the first was a box, this is a person, and the way the line finds a likeness is the method of the whole room. The fangs should be frightening and are not. This is someone laughing too hard at their own joke, and the room starts in good company.
A face with round purple glasses and a small red mouth, its hair yellow and blue scribble, drawn in loops of every color on a pale ground, a face caught mid-sentence.

A face in a storm of magenta line. Twenty-eight strokes make the whole drawing, but each stroke is long, looping across the square again and again, and the face is found where the line turns blue and green: two eyes, a nose, a closed mouth. The face does not stand out from the tangle. It is the tangle, looked at long enough. The mouth is closed and the eyes are level, and of all the faces in the Faces this is the calmest. It is a picture of someone thinking, drawn by not deciding where the thinking stops.
A head on red with two square goggle eyes, a big grin of pointed white teeth, two ears, and orange spiky hair, drawn in green and blue scribble, delighted and slightly deranged.

A screaming head in a halo of white bands. The face is green and teal scribble with two dark eyes, a nose and an open mouth with white teeth, and around it concentric bands of white and green run to the edges like ripples. The bands are the only calm thing in the picture. The series' first scream, from November 26, 2021, and it is not a scream of pain: the eyes are half shut and the bands around the head are the sound going out into the room. This is someone yelling with happiness, and the whole square rings with it.
November 27 to December 6, 2021. Eight heads in ten days: a man in a hat, a girl in a cap, white fur, blond scribble, confetti. The tangle is at its thickest and its friendliest.
A grinning face in purple, orange and yellow scribble, with a brow of dense black loops and a small open mouth, sly and pleased.
A man in a wide-brimmed hat, drawn in dark purple and yellow scribble so dense the face is almost solid, on a pale ground, the one face in the room that looks tired already.
A spiky dark head on pink with X marks for eyes and a frown, drawn in green, brown and red scribble, the first cross face in the room, sulking on the brightest ground.

A girl in a yellow cap and round glasses, inside a frame of pink, yellow and cyan lines, her hair falling in pink and black scribble. The cap is drawn as a box of yellow loops with a brim. Her mouth is a small red mark. It is the only framed work in the room and the only one where the scribble is held inside an edge. She is also the only face here that is not performing. She is just under her cap, looking out, and the frame around her is the closest the series comes to tenderness.

A grinning face covered in white fur, the hair and beard drawn in short white and lilac strokes standing out in every direction, with a wide grin of white teeth and small eyes. The ground is orange and yellow loops. The fur is the scribble turned into hair, and the grin is the widest in the room. It is a grin with nothing behind it but more fur, and that is the joke: the whole creature is hair and teeth, and it could not be happier about it.
A head of blond scribble with two dark eyes and a mouth of white block teeth in a red box, on a ground of colored bands, the box-head mouth dropped into a tangle head, and the result is startled.
A head on maroon with big ears, two target eyes, and red lips drawn in white and yellow line over red scribble, all ears and all eyes, listening hard.

A face in confetti. Small dabs of orange, blue, pink and green cover the whole square, and a small face sits in the middle of them with two dark eyes and a red mouth. The dabs are not loops; each one is a short stroke, and there are more than a thousand of them. Its 1,020 recorded strokes are the most of any work in the Faces. All that confetti, and the face in the middle of it is small and serious, with its mouth shut. The party is everywhere except on the face, and that is the picture.
December 6, 2021 to April 2022. Seven heads, spaced weeks apart. The scribble turns to hatching, the mouths open, and the faces stop being glad to see you.

A screaming egg of a head on brown, drawn in blue and cyan scribble, its mouth a wide open oval with white teeth, ten days after the scream in the halo, and this time there is no halo and no joy in it.

A face on purple with long lashes, angry brows and a snarl, painted in yellow and brown with scribble over it. The eyes are white with green irises under thick black lashes. The mouth is open on a row of white teeth, the lip pulled up. Below the face the body is a dark mass of black and yellow hatching. The face is painted first and the scribble is drawn on top, a change from the earlier rooms where the scribble was the face. It is also the first face in the room that is simply angry, with no grin hidden in it. The brows do it. Everything the autumn scribble found by accident, this face means.
A face on yellow with brown hair, blue eyes under dark lashes, and a snarl of white teeth, painted an hour after the purple one, and just as angry, with the light turned up.
A profile on dark blue with closed eyes, the face in white and red scribble, the hair a mass of red and black loops, the one head here turned away, as if the room had become too loud.
A hatched head on orange with yellow X marks for eyes and a thin grin of white teeth, drawn in brown, green and black hatching, the grin gone thin and the eyes gone.

A tall screaming face on pink and purple, its mouth open on two rows of white fangs, its eyes red rings, with a second face behind it at the right. The line is black and white with yellow and blue over it. A month after the snarl on purple, the mouth has opened all the way and the face has doubled. The second face is the first face's shadow, and it is screaming too. Set this beside the shout of joy in the white halo from November and the room's whole arc is there: the same open mouth, four months apart, and nothing left to be glad about.

A bearded face on orange with square glasses and a grimace of white teeth, the beard drawn in green and white hatching: the man in glasses from the first day of the room, back in April, and no longer laughing.

In the magenta storm the scribble is everything and the face is barely there, and it is at peace. On the purple snarl the face is painted and the scribble only sits on top, and it is furious. The line did the same work in both. What changed between November and February is what the line found when it looked.

Faces with weight, and for the first time in the collection, faces with someone behind them. The twenty works in this room are painted, not outlined: the cheek catches light, the eye sits in a socket, the chin casts a shadow. They come in two runs. In the winter of 2022 a set of quiet portraits, pale and soft, drawn in loops over discs of color. In the spring a set of glossy sculpted heads on flat bright grounds, shining like polished wood. The winter faces are the tenderest work in the Faces. The spring heads are the mask coming back, with a shine on it.

The ground changes with the paint, and so does the distance. The winter faces float in haze, with no edge between the face and the air, and three strokes in four are translucent, the most in the whole wing. You are close to them, the way you are close to someone across a table. The spring heads stand on one color, teal, orange, cyan, and their edges are hard. You are looking at an object on a shelf.

In the winter portraits the eyes look at you, or down, or away, and the mouths are closed. In the spring heads the eyes narrow, cross and hollow out, and the mouth starts to sneer. The glossy heads were drawn in the weeks the crypto market broke: the Terra collapse of May 9 to 13, 2022 falls between the mask with yellow beads and the head caught in the beams. The drawings do not mention it. They do not have to. This is the room where the collection shows what it can do when it stops performing, and then, as the money around it fell, decides to perform again, harder.
December 2021 and January 2022. A pale head in orange light, a face on black, and two portraits in haze. The paint arrives, and with it the first faces that are not laughing or biting.

A pale head in a glow of orange and red, its eyes crooked, one higher than the other, its teeth hanging from the lower edge of the face like a row of keys. The head is drawn in white, green and pink loops over soft discs of color, and the light seems to come from behind it. It is the first painted face in the series, from December 6, 2021, and the one that sets the room's method: discs of soft color first, then loops of line. The crooked eyes and the hanging teeth should make it a monster. The glow makes it a saint. This is the first face in the collection that asks for sympathy instead of a laugh.

A face on black with a white band across the brow like a cap, a thick mustache, and a mouth open on white teeth, painted in purple, orange and blue on Christmas Eve, a card from someone who does not do cards.

A ghostly face in pale grey and lilac, with two dark hollow eyes and a small mouth, drawn in thin loops over discs of white and pink. The hair is pale strokes falling at the sides. Nothing is outlined. The face is made only of where the discs are lighter and darker, and the line on top is thin and loose. Three quarters of its strokes are translucent and it carries sixty-three colors, more than any other work in the wing. All of that effort goes into a face that is barely there, with the eyes of someone who has not slept. It is the first picture in the Faces that is sad on purpose.
A woman with blue eyes and a small mouth, painted in olive and brown over soft discs, her hair loose at the sides, looking out at you with the plainest, most direct gaze in the wing.
January 26 to March 25, 2022. Eight faces in shadow: a bald man, a profile in loops, a lace collar, a hat and goggles, a man with his eyes closed. The stillest weeks in the collection.

A bald man's head in dark brown and gold, with green eyes that look off to one side, a straight nose and a closed mouth. The light falls from the left, so the brow and the near cheek are gold and the far side of the face sinks into dark. A thin orange line follows the eyes and the lips. Four strokes in five are translucent, the most in the room. It is the stillest face in the series, and the most like a person seen in a room. He is not performing anything. He is waiting, and the room waits with him. If the collection has a single picture of patience, it is this one.
A profile in loose white and black loops on cream, facing right, with an orange mouth and no teeth, forty-four strokes over soft discs of pink and lilac, dripping at the chin, a face half remembered.

A dark head on white, tilted back with the chin raised, modelled in brown and black with red, green and white loops over it, its eyes narrowed: the one face in these weeks that looks down at you, and does not think much of what it sees.

A long-haired figure in olive with dark eyes and a white lace collar, the collar drawn as a net of white lines and dots, the hair falling straight: a formal portrait, with the sitter's eyes lost in shadow and the collar doing all the talking.
A grey head in a hat with two huge pale eyes like goggles, a grin of white teeth, modelled in grey and purple, the cartoon grin dropped into the painted room and looking slightly lost there.

A man with his eyes closed, painted in brown and grey with orange and white line, on a ground of grey stripes, the one face in the Faces that has shut its eyes to the viewer, and the room's most private picture.

A dark face on magenta with a mop of pink and gold hair and a red X in one eye, outlined in thick white, its mouth a grid of small teeth: the X eye and the grille are back, and the room's quiet is over.
April 13 to May 22, 2022. Eight heads that shine: sculpted in dark paint, lit from one side, on flat bright grounds. The people are gone and the objects are back, polished and grinning.

A glossy dark head on violet with one yellow eye and a wide grin of white teeth, drawn in white and black line over paint that shines. A row of white teeth sits on top of the head like a crown. The nose is a long triangle. It is the first of the glossy heads, from April 13, 2022, and it casts a shadow on the violet, the first shadow in the room. The shadow is what makes it an object. After the winter's faces, which had no edges, this one has a hard edge, a shine and a crown of teeth, and the grin is the box-head grin, back on a head that has been carved and varnished.
A glossy head on orange with narrowed eyes and a sneer, painted in brown, gold and black with scribble over the crown, the first sneer in the Faces, and it suits the shine.

A glossy dark head on lavender with a yellow cross in one eye and a target in the other, a grin of white teeth, and fingers resting on top of the head, as if someone were holding the mask up to show it.

A glossy dark mask on a ground of orange and pink stripes, with two swirl eyes, a long nose, a row of large white teeth and a border of yellow beads around the head. The paint is black with white and blue highlights, and the beads are small yellow circles drawn at even spacing. The stripes behind it run in waves. With 372 recorded strokes it is the most worked of the glossy heads. It is a mask in the plain sense: a carved face with beads around the edge and nothing behind it, and the swirl eyes stare because they cannot do anything else. The winter faces looked at you. This one is for looking at.
A glossy green head in a hat with flowers on the brim, on olive, with small eyes and an open mouth, a mask dressed for a wedding.

A glossy face on cyan with crooked eyes, one high and one low, a row of white teeth, and a crown of yellow scribble for hair, the crooked eyes of the first painted head back in April, with the softness gone.

A glossy dark head on orange, lit by pale beams from the upper left, its mouth open on white teeth, one eye a white ring in shadow. The beams are soft wedges of pale yellow laid over the head. Five months after the pale head in the orange glow, the light is back, but now it falls on something solid and casts a shadow. The last work in the room, from May 22, 2022, and the last of the numbered Faces, drawn nine days after Terra's collapse and five weeks after the collector bought his first n n x y z ink. The first painted face dissolved in the light. This one is caught in it, mouth open, like something found with a torch. That is the distance the series travelled in five months: from a face the light passes through to a face the light catches.

The pale head in the orange glow is lit from behind, and the face is barely solid. The dark head from May is lit by beams, and it is all solid. In both, the light is the subject. In the first it dissolves the face, and what is left is gentle. In the last it strikes it, and what is left is a mask with its mouth open. Between them sit eight people who were simply painted, and the room is quietest where it is best.

Fear, drawn as a face. The twenty works in this room share a ground of black or near-black, and out of it the drawing pulls a head: a halo of ochre, a white line, a pair of lit eyes, a grille of teeth. They run from December 2021 to April 2022, and December was the darkest month of the whole collection, with two grounds in three laid down black.

These are the skulls and the hooded things, and the room does not pretend they are anything else. But look at how they are made and the fear turns out to be a game the artist is playing with you. In some works the black is a flat ground and the head is a few white lines on it, a skull in twenty-six strokes with the artist's own name written where its eyes should be. In others the black is paint, and a head is modelled out of it with highlights until it shines like a lamp in a cellar. The first kind is a cartoon of death. The second is a portrait of it.

Watch the teeth. They are nearly the only white in most of these pictures and they are what the eye finds first: a zipper, a grille, four fangs, a row of pegs hanging from a jaw. Every one of these mouths is a grin and a threat at once, and the room never says which. That is the flaw the artist built in on purpose, and it is why these faces keep you looking.
Four works from December 4 to 6, 2021, the week the dark grounds begin. A head in an ochre halo, a black head on white, a blue head lit from inside, and a face in a pink frame.

A head on black inside a halo of ochre, with two target eyes in yellow rings, a white zigzag along the brow, and a mouth of white teeth drawn like a zipper. Inside the head the fill is colored scribble, cyan, pink and yellow, with black line over it. The halo is the only soft thing in the picture, a band of brown that keeps the head from falling into the black. This is the series' first dark work, and the zipper mouth is the whole room in one mark: it is a smile until you notice it is also closed.
A black head on a white ground, one ringed eye and one boxed eye, a long nose, and a grille of grey teeth in a red mouth, the one head here that stands in daylight and is no less a skull for it.

A dark blue head with two yellow slit eyes and a grin of white teeth, painted in blue and black with white highlights along the crown. Half its strokes are translucent, more than any other work in the room, and the light they build comes from the upper left, picking out the brow and leaving the jaw in shadow. The eyes glow in their sockets like something awake in a dark room. The grin curves up at the right. It is the first painted head in the Faces that shines, and the first that watches you back.
A face in a frame of pink loops on dark red, one eye a sun of orange rays and the other an arched box, with a grille of white teeth at the bottom: a shrine with a mouth.
January 21 to February 9, 2022. Seven works in three weeks, and the room's two ways of drawing fear side by side: skulls in a few strokes of line, and hooded figures with almost no face at all.
A skull drawn in yellow and orange loops over a curtain of dark vertical strokes, three quarters of them translucent, so that the ghost is mostly veil and the teeth are what is solid.
A face drawn in white and red line on dark red, with X marks in both eyes, spiky lashes and a small mouth of fangs, in forty-seven strokes: the eyes are cancelled and the mouth is still open.

A tall head on dark teal with two starburst eyes under spiky lashes, a green cross for a nose, and a mouth of five white teeth in a box. The head is drawn in white, orange and cyan line over soft vertical strokes of blue and grey, so it stands in rain. The two eyes are different, a white disc at the left and an orange ring at the right, and the mismatch gives the face the look of someone caught mid-thought. The cross on the nose is drawn in green zigzag. Of all the heads in the room this is the one that is not afraid and not frightening; it is just standing there, getting wet.

A black mass of hair on grey, and in it a face: two white eyes with dark pupils, a short line for a nose, and four white fangs. Twenty-three recorded strokes, the fewest in the room. The hair is drawn as a few loops of white line over black, and the black is one shape. The whole face is the eyes and the fangs, and they are enough. This is fear at its cheapest and most effective, the thing under the bed drawn by someone who knows exactly how little it takes.

A hooded skull on black, drawn in white line with a red hood, and the letters N N X Y Z written in red across its brow and its eyes. Two rows of white teeth sit below. Two hands rest at the bottom in red outline. Twenty-six strokes. The letters are the artist's name, and they sit on the skull where the eyes should be, so the name does the looking. Death in a hood is the oldest cartoon there is, and the artist signs it across the face: this is me, and I am grinning.
A hooded figure on black, its hood and shoulders outlined with yellow dots like a fairground sign, a white face with one sun-burst eye and one red star eye, and a grille of white teeth in a red box.
A hooded head painted in orange and brown, with no face at all except a wide grin of white teeth in the dark of the hood, and the grin is enough to make the dark a face.
February 12 to 21, 2022. A horned head, a skull with pink eyes lit by beams, a skull with blue eyes that look wet, and a bird skull. The beams that will light the whole of May arrive here first.
A horned dark head on green, two tall white eyes under a heavy brow and a grille of yellow teeth, drawn in black and blue scribble over soft green blobs, a devil who looks more worried than wicked.

A skull with two huge pink eyes, each a ring of magenta rays around a white center, lit by pale beams that cross the square from the upper left. The skull is drawn in black and colored line over dark, and the mouth is a row of white triangle teeth in a dark box. The beams are the first in the Faces, soft bands laid over everything, and where they fall the lines show through them. Three months later they will light nearly every drawing in May. Here they fall on a skull, and the skull looks dazzled, not dead.

A skull painted in pink, brown and grey on black, with two blue eyes in dark sockets, each a ring of blue with a white highlight, and a row of white teeth hanging from the jaw at the lower right. Nothing is outlined; two strokes in three are translucent and the skull is modelled from them with a thin white edge. Where the blue head of December glowed from inside, this one is lit from the front, and the eyes look wet. A skull cannot cry, and this one looks as if it is about to. It is the saddest picture in the room, and the most carefully painted.
A bird skull with a long beak, drawn in black, white, red and cyan strokes on dark brown, a brush of pale lines hanging from the jaw like a beard: the only skull here that is not a person.

March 16 to April 25, 2022. Five heads, and the dark ground is now a stage: a box with an X eye, a chunky head with a heart for an eye, a head of blocks, a glossy bald head screaming, and a skull with its jaw off.

A chunky head on dark grey with a red heart in a box for an eye, a box of white teeth, and two more boxes of teeth at the bottom like feet, in confetti scribble: the heart is crossed with a yellow bar, and the head is cheerful anyway.

A head built from stacked blocks on dark navy, one eye in a tilted box and the other a cluster of rings, a long bar of white teeth at the bottom, a face assembled like a machine and worried like a person.

A glossy bald head on black, its skin a weave of colored scribble, two ringed eyes, and a mouth thrown open on white teeth, one side of the head lit white: the room's one scream, and it is drawn in party colors.

A glossy skull on pink with spiky hair, one huge yellow eye, and its jaw come off, lying below the teeth as a separate row. The skull is painted in gold and black with white highlights, and the teeth hang from the upper jaw in a row of long pegs. Two months after the skull with blue eyes, the modelled skull is back, and this time it has come apart. The pink ground is the brightest in the room and the picture is the room's most broken. The last work here, from April 25, 2022, and the grin has finally fallen off the face.

Look again at the hooded skull with the letters across its eyes, twenty-six strokes on black, and then at the glossy skull on pink with its jaw on the floor. One is nothing but line, and it is laughing at you. The other is modelled, lit and broken, and it is not. Both are skulls in the dark, and both make you look at the teeth, which is where this collection decides whether a face is joking.

Sparer faces on flat color, and the sparer they get, the lighter they feel. The twenty works in this room are drawn with less: a cartoon head in a few strokes, a mask of beads and petals, a diagram of a face in colored line with the ground showing through. Most are from the first four months of 2022, the same months as the skulls and the quiet portraits. This is the artist taking a breath between them.

The line does different things here. On some works it is a cartoon outline, thick and black, with a flat color inside. On others it is a diagram, drawing each part of the face as a shape and leaving the rest to the ground. And on one, the grey face with glasses, it is eight loops and nothing else. Whatever the line does, the ground does the rest, and the grounds are the brightest in the wing: lime, orange, yellow, teal. The color carries the mood, and the mood is a shrug and a grin.

In the earlier rooms the ground is filled or scribbled until the square is full. Here the drawing sits on it like a sticker. Half the canvas is often left bare, and that bareness is the feeling of the room: nothing to hide, nothing to bury, a face put down and left alone. It is the one room in the Faces where the teeth are nearly always a joke.
December 2021 to February 2022. A scribble mask on white, then a run of cartoon heads: goggle eyes on lime, a black head on red, a face with a peace sign. The line gets thick and the faces get funny.

An oval mask on white in cyan, pink and green scribble, with two eyes looking up, red lips, and a grin of white teeth, drawn on December 3, 2021, the tangle's method on the bare ground of this room, and the first face here to look pleased about nothing in particular.

A yellow-green face on lime, hatched in yellow and blue, with two goggle eyes in white boxes under a dark brow and a row of white teeth hanging from the chin. The face is a cartoon: a thick outline, a flat color, two boxes for eyes. The teeth hang below the jaw as a row of white pegs, like the pale head in the painted room, but drawn in line. The cartoon run begins here. The same hanging teeth that made the painted head a saint make this one a goof, and the difference is nothing but the ground: lime instead of a glow.

A grey mask inside a ring of yellow dots, with two white-dot eyes in dark boxes, a row of pink dots on the brow, and a mouth drawn as a grate of dark bars. Around the yellow dots, rings of grey scallops run to the edges like the rim of a shield. The mask is drawn in soft grey and teal with thin orange line, and it is the most ordered drawing in the room: every mark is a dot, a ring or a bar. The grate of a mouth is the one unfriendly thing in it, and the shield around it says why: this face is armour, and it is calm because nothing gets in.
A black cartoon head on red, with two white eye boxes and small pupils, a red nose, a wide grin of white teeth, and white marks at the corners like motion lines, a face that has just heard good news.

A mask head on yellow filled with colored scribble, two white slots for eyes with red slits inside, and a grimace of white teeth in a red mouth, the first face here that is not enjoying itself, and it is still on yellow.

A black head and shoulders on pink and purple, with a yellow X in one eye, an orange X in the other, small white fangs, and a black hand raised at the right in a peace sign. The figure is one flat black shape outlined in cyan, and the X marks are the only color on it. Seventy-four strokes. It is the one work in the room with a gesture, and the gesture settles the room's question: crossed eyes, fangs, and two fingers up for peace. The threat and the joke are the same figure, and it is waving at you.

February 19 to March 6, 2022. A skull with a crown for an eye, an owl, a gold blob with star eyes, a skull in profile, a sun of petals and beads, and an angular head in a haze. Emblems, not people: things you could stamp on a flag.

A cartoon skull in white line under cyan rays, with a yellow crown in a box for one eye and a window of red grid for the other, a grille of white teeth and lime fingers at the side, a skull that has made it to royalty and is pleased to be seen.

An owl head on orange with pointed ears, two green ringed eyes crossed with red, and a grille of white bars for a mouth, drawn in black, blue and yellow hatching: the box-head mouth on a bird, and the bird looks startled to have it.
A gold blob of a head curved like a banana on green diagonal stripes, with two red star eyes and a grin of white fangs, the silliest shape in the wing, grinning like it knows.

A skull in profile on teal, drawn in white and black line, with a sunflower for an eye, a crest of yellow loops, and a grid of thin lines over the whole square, a skull on graph paper, measured and cheerful.

A sun of a mask on dark green: a round face ringed with yellow petals, each with a dot, and a row of red spikes along the top like a crown. One eye is a white dot in a dark socket, the other a ring with a white center. The mouth is white teeth in a dark oval. Beads of blue, pink and yellow run around the face. With 347 recorded strokes it is the most worked drawing in the room, and the only one with every part in its place. It is a sun that has been up too long: the petals are tidy, the crown is on, and the mouth under them is open in something between a smile and a groan. The room's emblem of effort, drawn as a face that has had enough of being an emblem.

An angular head on a neck, drawn in black, white and blue line over a haze of soft gold and brown discs, its face a few straight strokes, the quiet portraits' haze with a cartoon drawn on it, and the one head here that is thinking.
March 24 to April 16, 2022. Seven faces drawn as diagrams, from eight grey loops to a machine of rings and teeth on teal. The line stops pretending to be anything but line.

A face in eight grey loops on grey: two circles for glasses, a curl for a nose, a spiral for a mouth, and a cluster of pink and orange bubbles for hair. Fifty-eight strokes, each one a quick mark, make the sparest drawing in the whole collection. Nothing is filled and nothing is scribbled. It is the sparest face in the Faces, and the most contented. The spiral mouth could be a smile or a hum. After four months of teeth, here is a face with none, and it needs none.

A head of dark red scribble on grey with two yellow ex eyes, a blue bar falling from the face like a tear, and an orange band across the top, the one sad drawing in the room, and the sadness is a single blue stripe.

A flat face on yellow, striped in blue, green and orange, with two pink X marks for eyes, four small dots across the brow, and a thick white outline with rays. At the lower right a small red face on a stick looks on with its own ex eyes. The stripes run down the face and drip at the chin. The outline is drawn with short strokes standing out from it like a child's sun. The big face is solemn, with its mouth shut and its eyes crossed out, and the little face on the stick beside it is grinning. The picture has brought its own heckler.

A face on navy drawn in blue, pink and yellow line: a ringed eye in a box, a box with an X, a yellow crest, and a long white zigzag of teeth across the lower face, the kit of parts floated on dark, and the zigzag is a laugh.

A face on olive in white, orange and blue line, with a ringed eye and a spiky eye, two rows of hanging teeth, and a chain of white teeth across the bottom, more teeth than face, and all of them cheerful.

A face on teal with two eyes like propellers in rings, a red ball for a nose, a bar of white teeth in a red box, and a crown of yellow and blue ovals. Everything is drawn in line, and every part is a separate shape: a ring, a box, a ball, a bar. Three weeks after the face in eight grey loops, this is the diagram with all its parts filled in. The last work in the room, from April 16, 2022. The propeller eyes spin and the red nose is a clown's, and the whole machine is built to be looked at and liked. The room ends on the kit assembled as a toy, which is where the Faces began.

Look again at the face in eight grey loops, and then at the face of propellers and teeth on teal. Both are line on a flat ground. One leaves almost everything out and is at peace with it. The other draws every part and still leaves the ground showing. That is the range of this room: from a face that needs nothing to a face that has everything and is still not sure it is a face.

Box heads with their eyes struck through. In this room the eye is an X, a red cross, a plus sign, or a letter, and the box head of the first room comes back with its eyes cancelled. Twenty-six works, from December 1, 2021 to March 18, 2022, and then the collection piece, number zero zero zero zero, made in July. The grin from the first room is still here, under every crossed eye, and that is the room's unease: a face that cannot see you and is still smiling.

The cross is drawn many ways. A red X over a ring. A plus sign in a white box. Two red bars. And in a handful of works the eyes spell the artist's name: an X in one box, a Y in the next, a Z in the third. The letters N, N, X, Y and Z appear as eyes, as a brow, and on number 48 as the whole face. An X for an eye is the cartoonist's sign for dead, or drunk, or knocked out. The artist takes that sign and makes it a signature. The name is in the eyes, so the one thing the face cannot do is look. Anyone who knows Jean-Michel Basquiat will see him here: the crowns, the crossed eyes, the words written into the face, the name as the subject. The gallery makes the comparison; the artist has not. What the two share is the habit of signing the picture from inside it.

Watch the mouth under the crossed eyes. It is almost always a grid of white block teeth in a box, and as the eyes get stranger the teeth stay the same. Blind and grinning, head after head, until the room ends on the one work that puts every mark in the series into a single square, with the name drawn large and no face at all.

December 1 to 6, 2021. Eight box heads, the first with green crosses in its eyes, the last with the artist's name written across the whole face. Six days, and the eye goes from target to cross to letter.

A box head inside a white box frame on green, with two ringed eyes crossed by green plus signs, a V of red and white for a nose, and bands of yellow and red filling the face. Two small boxes with spirals sit at the sides like ears. It is the first crossed eye in the series, from December 1, 2021, drawn not as a cancellation but as a plus sign laid over a target. A plus is an addition, and the face is still fine: the teeth are in their box and the ears are on. The room starts with the cross as a decoration. It does not stay one.
A rounded box head on dark teal in cyan and red scribble, two red crosses in blue eye boxes, and a mouth of white triangle teeth, the crosses gone red and the teeth gone sharp, four days in.
A box head on white in magenta and yellow scribble, two orange crosses in white eye boxes, and white block teeth in a tilted box, the same head in daylight, and no less blind for it.

A block head on blue stripes with two orange ringed eyes crossed in white, and a mouth open on two rows of white teeth, upper and lower, the widest grin in the chapter on the only face that has lost both eyes to white.
A horned owl mask on blue with a yellow zigzag crown, a white X in one eye and a dot in the other, and a grille of white teeth in a red box, one eye out and one eye open, and the open one is wary.

The artist's name as a face. The letters N and N sit at the top in white, X Y Z in a box below them, a plus sign in cyan beside them, and a cross in a ring at the right. Below, a row of white ovals for teeth and a second row of ovals under a yellow wave. On purple and blue with yellow bars. Nothing here is a nose or a cheek; the face is made entirely of the name and its marks. Six days into the room, the artist has already drawn the conclusion: if the eyes are letters, the face is a signature. The teeth stay, two rows of them, because a signature in this collection still has to grin.

A dark square with neon slashes of lime, red, pink and blue across it, a pink X in one eye and a heart in the other, and a brown drip running down the center of the face. The mouth is a pink bar at the bottom. Where the name was drawn as a face a few hours earlier, here the marks have been thrown at the square: the X is a slash, the slashes are the face, and the drip runs through all of it. One eye is crossed and the other is a heart, and the drip between them is the only thing in the room that looks like it hurt. The angriest picture in the Faces, and it was made the same evening as the signature.
December 31 to February 8. Six heads over five weeks, with red crosses, plus signs and target eyes, and long fangs. The cross settles in, and the grins get longer in the tooth.
A box head with coils at the sides like springs, two triangle eyes with red crosses, a big grid of white teeth, drawn on the last day of 2021, wound up and grinning into the new year.

A box head on grey with two pink boxes for eyes, each with a white plus sign, a row of big white block teeth in a red box, and a comb of yellow and black spikes along the top for a crown. Drawn on the morning of January 1, 2022, in ninety-four strokes. A month after the first green crosses, the plus sign has become the whole eye: a white cross in a pink box, nothing else. New Year's morning, a crown, a grin, and no eyes at all. It is the room's cheerfulness at its most unsettling, and the artist drew it first thing.
A head on yellow and white with a sunflower for one eye, green petals around a target, and a red cross for the other, two boxes of white teeth side by side, one eye in bloom and one eye out.

A box head on dark brown with a red cross in one eye and a red X in the other, long white fangs in a dark mouth, and yellow wavy marks floating on the ground, the fangs the longest in the room, and the face still cannot see what it is baring them at.
A box head on orange in pink and blue line, a red cross in one eye and a red X in the other, a grille of white teeth in a red box, and a crest of yellow strokes, bright, blind and cheerful.
February 9 to 20, 2022. The eyes become letters. Six heads in which an X, a Y and a Z sit where the eyes should be. The face is now a word, and the word is the artist.

A box head on lavender with three boxes in a row for eyes, and in them an X, a Y and a Z in red. Below, two boxes of white teeth side by side and a third box of teeth at the bottom. Horns of red line stand at the top corners. The name has moved from the brow to the eyes, one letter to a box, and the head has three eyes to hold it. Three eyes, three boxes of teeth, two horns: it is a machine for displaying a name, and the name is all it can see. The friendliest-looking of the letter heads, and the most completely blind.
A box head on teal with a white X in one eye and a red cross in the other, a crown of yellow spikes, and a long bar of white teeth in a red box, crowned and cancelled.
A round head on orange and purple with two star ex eyes in boxes, a white nose, and a ring of white teeth around the chin like a collar, the teeth worn as jewellery now.

A head on magenta with a yellow X in one eye and a blue target in the other, a yellow Y for a nose, a grin of white teeth and a second small mouth under the left eye, the name taking over the nose as well, and a second mouth growing where an eye should be.

A box head on olive with three boxes for eyes in a row, X, Y and Z in red, a triangle for a nose like a house, a column of blue ovals, and a box of white teeth. Eleven days after the first three-eyed head, the letters are back in their boxes, and the head is built from blocks: a box for the eyes, a box for the nose, a box for the teeth. It is the tidiest head in the room, every part in a drawer, and the tidiness is the point: a face filed away under its own name.
A box head with a yellow hat brim and red ex eyes stands on a post like a sign, on orange: the face has become a signpost, and the sign says the name.
February 27 to March 18, 2022, five last box heads, and then the collection piece, drawn in July, which gathers every mark in the series into one square.
A box head on purple standing on two posts, with two eyes of red bars in boxes, a yellow crest, and a long bar of white teeth, a face on stilts, out of reach and grinning down.

A box head on yellow with goggles, two white ovals joined by a bar, each with a red cross, and a wide grin of white teeth, the goggles the last joke in the series: lenses for eyes that are crossed out behind them.

A box head on maroon with a red and white X in a cyan box for one eye and a slash in the other, orange horns, a long nose, and a grin of white teeth, the last of the crossed boxes, from March 18, 2022, horned and blind and still pleased.

The collection piece, an edition of one, drawn on July 20, 2022, four months after the last numbered face. A dense square of pattern: the letters N, N, X, Y and Z drawn large in the center, a red heart at the top, a flower at the right, beads, zigzags, grids and teeth filling every corner. With 753 recorded strokes it is the most worked drawing in the Faces. The name that was a face in December is here the whole picture, and there is no face left around it: no eyes to cross, no mouth to grin, only the heart above the letters and the rows of teeth at the bottom edge, where they have become a border. The artist held this one back and sold it last, as the key to the complete set. Jamie Thingelstad bought it, and with it the artist sent the Faces that had not sold, so that the set on these walls is the whole series. The picture says what the sale says. The series is over, and what remains is the signature, the heart, and the teeth.

The first crossed eyes were green plus signs on a box head in December, and the head was grinning. The last work is the collection piece, where the letters of the name fill the square and there is no mouth left to grin with. The X started as a mark on an eye. By July it was the subject, and the subject was the artist, signing off on a series that could no longer see.

For ten weeks in the spring of 2022 the same formula held: one flat color, one black shape, and a ring of short wavy lines. Twenty-eight works came out of it, from a snarling cat on March 25 to a cat the size of a hill on June 2. These are the friendliest drawings n n x y z made all year, and they were made in the busiest ten weeks of the artist's life on the board, when the inks were selling, the airdrops were going out, and more than seventy works went by in a single month.

Inside the black there is almost nothing. A pair of spiral eyes, or two small X marks, and sometimes a row of jagged teeth. A spiral makes a cat dizzy or wild. An X closes an eye for good, and the same X on a rabbit, a bee and a whole crowd of heads runs through the room like a signature. The wavy lines are the other constant. They sit in the color around the figure, never touching it, and they make a still black shape hum, as if every creature here were giving off heat.

The cats and the scarecrows had a second life. On May 1 the artist told collectors that whoever held certain inks by the middle of the month would receive new work on another chain, and in July the cats became the chic city cat club, a Polygon collection of nearly ten thousand cats, one sent free to every holder and the rest offered for a single MATIC. The whole room came to the collector at once: twenty-seven of these works were sent to Jamie Thingelstad's wallet on October 16, 2022, the day after the series ended. Watch the black horizon arrive under the creatures, watch the figures turn hairy, and watch, in the last days, the black become nearly all there is.
The room begins with four cats. The first arrives in March, the other three in one week of April, and between them they set every rule the next ten weeks will follow.

A black cat arches over a scribbled yellow and white ground, its back one long diagonal across the square. The eyes are two red spirals in orange boxes, and the mouth is a white zigzag of teeth. Thick blue wavy lines fill the teal around it. It is the first black silhouette in the collection, from March 25, 2022, and the only one that snarls. The artist posted it to X the same day with a link to the ink, the way nearly every work in this wing was announced: a title, a number, and the address on the board. Everything that follows in the room is this cat with the anger taken out.
The same cat lies on a black ledge with its tail up, and nothing is drawn inside it but two yellow spirals and two white fangs.

One day later the same cat lies on the same ledge, facing the other way. Its body is filled with yellow scribble, so the black shows only at the edges, and the cat turns from a cut-out into something lit from inside. The eyes are red targets with crosses. Set it beside the cat from the day before and the whole method of the room is visible: a black shape is a decision about what to leave out, and filling it back in makes a different animal.
Balanced on a black ball, a cat curls its tail over its head, with blue spiral eyes and a white saw-tooth grin.

Six works in three days, April 25 to 27. The cat gives way to other creatures, a black horizon appears under them, and two are set inside a frame. On April 25 the artist also minted a drawing called 200 nifties, to mark two hundred inks on the board, straight into the collector's wallet, the first n n x y z work he was given.

Two cats sit facing each other on a red ground, and between them a heart made of two black bars meets at its point. Both have yellow spiral eyes and a jagged yellow grin. Yellow lines fill the red in rings around them. Two cats and a heart is the gentlest picture in the series, and it was made on April 25, the day the artist celebrated two hundred inks on the board and sent the celebration piece to the collectors who had been paying attention. The affection in the drawing and the affection in the gesture are the same thing.
Inside a white frame, a black bear hugs its round belly in the corner of a yellow square, with no wavy lines at all.
No horizon under this one. A black bird with one yellow spiral eye and a zigzag beak floats on teal.

After three weeks away, the black turns hairy. Scarecrows are drawn in bristling strokes, grass grows along the horizon, and the X mark arrives for the eyes. These are the inks the artist named in the May airdrop: hold a cat or a scarecrow, and something new would follow.
On a single pole, a scarecrow holds its arms out, drawn in scratchy strokes, with grass bristling along the black horizon and every wavy line in black on orange.

The scarecrow again, a day later, now standing in a field with a black cat beside a purple fence. Its face has two round yellow eyes and its body is a mass of hatched strokes. Yellow wavy marks are everywhere in the magenta. This is the drawing that gave the room's two formulas to each other: the hairy scarecrow and the flat cat share one field. The artist promised the scarecrow holders their own collection and, as late as July 31, was still telling them it had not been forgotten. The cats got their club; the scarecrows are still waiting at the fence.
A rabbit sits upright on red with both ears straight up, its eyes two X marks and its mouth a small zigzag, a line down its chest like a seam.
Dancing on one leg, a round-headed figure bends its arms, ex eyes, the wavy lines black again on orange.

A witch in a pointed hat stirs a cauldron from a step ladder, and the cauldron says Scaffold eeth in scratchy pale letters. The witch is drawn like the scarecrows, in bristling strokes with one X for an eye, and sparks rise from the pot. Scaffold-ETH is the open-source toolkit Nifty Ink was built with, made by Austin Griffith, the engineer who built the board. He was one of the artist's earliest buyers, and in February 2022 he put ether into the artist's Ethereum wallet so the inks could be upgraded to the main chain. This is the one drawing in the room about where the room came from: a witch cooking the thing that made her possible, and enjoying it.

The last week of May brings the small things: a snail, a turtle, a bee, a balloon, a worm, a spider, a flower and a crowd. Each gets one shape, one color and its ring of lines. Eight of them were drawn on two days, May 25 and 31.
Along the horizon crawls a snail with a yellow spiral shell and a tiny cat-like face.
Over the horizon a bee with ex eyes hovers, while a small black flower with spiral eyes looks up at it from the lower right.
On a long wavy string a balloon with spiral eyes and a jagged grin rises, and a black hand at the bottom corner lets it go.
Out of a bitten apple on a steep black slope rises a worm with ex eyes, the lines around it black on green.
From the top edge a spider hangs on a thin thread, legs tucked around a round body, three small yellow marks for a face.

A crowd of black heads fills the bottom of a yellow square, every face a pair of X marks. The yellow sits inside a thick black border, so the square is a window and the crowd stands at its sill. Not one of them has a mouth. It is the only crowd in the room, and it comes at the end of May, when the market had just fallen and the board was full of people wondering what they were holding. The ex eyes are the room's joke about being closed for good, and here there are twelve of them, all looking out of the same window, and nothing to see.

The room ends on June 1 and 2 with four works that take the formula in four directions: a figure drawn in scribble, a child reaching up, a page of tiny figures with no color at all, and one last enormous cat.
Bent over two crates marked with sunbursts, a scribbled figure rests its hands on the lids, while a small snail crosses the pink at the bottom left.

A figure seen from behind reaches up to a small black heart that gives off sparks. The face is turned away, and all that shows of it is one small X on the cheek. The wavy lines, black now, stand up along the arm and the head like hair on end. A child reaching for a spark is the most tender picture in the wing, and it was made on June 1, 2022, in the week the first part of the series ended. The heart is tiny and the yellow is enormous. Everything in the drawing is about the distance between the hand and the thing it wants.
Rows of tiny black figures tumble across a white page, each one scribbled in a few strokes, with a single red one beside the signature.

A cat the size of a hill crouches on a black slope, filling the square from edge to edge, and looks out with yellow spiral eyes and a stitched grin. Its tail rises off the top of the picture and comes back down. The blue outline is the same as the first cat's, the spirals are the same, and nothing else is. The first cat arched and snarled at the edge of a scribbled field; this one has grown until the field is gone. It is the last silhouette, from June 2, and the calmest. Ten weeks of black shapes end with the biggest of them, at rest.

Go back to the first cat and the last. The one from March arches and bares its teeth on a scribbled ground. The one from June fills the whole square and sits still, with the same blue outline and the same spiral eyes. Between them the room tried the formula on twenty-six other creatures and never once turned mean. In the rooms next door the eyes are lamps and the heads are skulls. Here, for ten weeks, the black shapes were simply glad to be on the block.

In this room the eyes are lamps. Twenty-one works from May 2022 share one device: a head or a creature whose eyes give off light, and a beam that crosses the square like a searchlight. Where the light lands, the drawing goes pale and the lines show through it. Where it does not, the ground stays dense, scribbled in olive, red and blue. Twelve of them came in five days, May 7 to 11, and those were the five days the crypto market broke. Terra's stablecoin lost its peg on May 9 and its coin went to nothing by the 12th; the artist drew a head with its eyes blazing every day of it.

The light takes two forms. In the framed heads it is a hard wedge, drawn as a solid band of pale yellow laid over everything, with a bright white disc where it starts. In the painted creatures, the bears and the hooded figure, it is a halo, soft at the edges, with round spots of glare floating in it like dust in a projector. Both kinds do the same work: they fix where you look and leave the rest of the head in shadow. A searchlight is a nervous thing. It belongs to someone who needs to see.

The words say what the eyes mean. One work is titled cash lightning, and the artist gave it away to the three buyers who had just carried the inks past fifteen hundred xDai in sales. A teddy bear has BULLISH on its chest; a wolf two days later says STILL BULLISH, and that one, number 100, was minted free into sixty-two wallets, the collector's among them. On May 12, with the market on the floor, the artist posted that it was the best time to upgrade the inks to the main chain, and the glowing eyes in this room are that sentence drawn: bright, fixed, and not entirely sure.

Six framed heads open the room, drawn between May 7 and 9. Each one is packed to the frame with marks, and each one is cut by a beam. Over the same weekend the artist passed fifteen hundred xDai in sales on the board and said thank you with the fourth work here.

A head tips to the right inside a tan frame, two square eyes glowing white, and a beam spills out of them toward the lower right corner. The mouth is a panel of upright teeth, lit from the same source. Around the head the ground is a weave of olive, yellow and blue scribble, with orange fence posts along the bottom. The light is drawn as a pale band laid over all of it, so the scribble shows through the beam like a pattern through gauze. It is the first lit head, from May 7, a Saturday. The beam does not come from anywhere; it comes from the eyes and goes out into the room, looking for something.
Turned on its side, a machine of a head: a bar of four round dials, a stack of triangles, a grid for a cheek, and beams crossing the whole thing on the diagonal.
One huge round eye on the left throws a wide beam down and to the right, past a small square eye and a grinning row of teeth.

The same head again, under green light. The drawing is the one from number 75 with the colors shifted: the beam is lime, the eye has a spiral in it, and the whole ground has gone cool. Its title is the only one in the room with words, cash lightning, and it was never for sale. On the evening of May 8 the artist thanked three collectors by name for helping to break the fifteen-hundred-xDai limit on the board and sent them this as an airdrop. Set the two heads side by side and the difference is the light alone, warm on one and acid on the other, falling on identical lines. The acid one is the thank-you note.
Under a glass dome on a round base, a small creature with two glowing eyes sits in a flood of yellow rays, the whole picture lit from behind it.
Two days, May 9 to 11, and six works. A furry creature appears twice, once with its eyes lit and once in the dark, and then the heads put on helmets. These are the days Terra fell.
A round, furry creature with two enormous glowing eyes squats on a patch of grass, orange stripes behind its head, its paws folded over its belly.

The same creature, half an hour later, with the lights off. It sits in plain black now, inside a white border, and its eyes are two dark spirals where the lamps were. The fur is the same hatching, the paws are the same, the belly has the same pale patch. Without the glow the creature looks smaller and more worried, and the drawing is mostly shadow. May 9, 2022, was the day the stablecoin began to slip. The artist drew a creature with its eyes burning and then, before the hour was out, the same creature in the dark. Nobody has to decide which one is the portrait of that day. The room keeps both.
In profile, facing left, a head sends two beams out of two square eyes, while a black band on the right edge holds the picture like a shoulder.
A creature with a yellow beak and a row of hanging teeth like icicles, its eyes two glowing leaf shapes, set in a frame of pale blue.
A blue head with a crest like a helmet, a wide grin of white teeth, and a single beam from a square eye at the upper left.
Painted, not scribbled: a helmeted figure in gold and black holds its hands together under a grinning mouth, lit by a wide beam from the upper left, on May 11, with the market still falling.

After nine days away the glow comes back bigger. From May 20 to 22 the eyes become whole lamps, and two of the creatures start to speak. On May 20 the collector bought the first of them, the head with wild hair, for fifteen xDai.

A head with a mop of wild yellow and black hair, a thin neck, and two orbs of light for eyes, each one larger than the mouth beneath it. Jamie Thingelstad bought it the day it was drawn, for fifteen xDai, his third purchase from the series.
A teddy bear with sparking antennae sits in a burst of orange rays, its eyes two small lamps and the word BULLISH written across its chest, ten days after the crash.
A head in white scribble over pink and orange, two beams driving to the right out of the eyes, three orange drips hanging from the top.
An armored figure in black and gold, with a visor and one red eye, points a finger under a sky of blue rays.

The room closes with the largest drawings in it: a hooded figure holding lights, a bear with glowing goggles, a wolf with a slogan that went out to sixty-two wallets, and a skull mask lit from inside.
Inside a dark frame a hooded, bearded figure with glowing eyes holds out a hand, and round spots of light float around it like bubbles.

A bear sits on a white ground, painted in soft grey and gold, its eyes hidden behind red goggles that glow. Two beams leave the goggles toward the lower left. On its shoulder, almost too small to see, stands a tiny figure. The bear is drawn with long, careful painted strokes, its paws resting on its knees, and the white around it is cloudy, not flat. At 817 recorded strokes, no other work in the room took as much drawing. It is the gentlest of the lit creatures: a bear that has sat down, and whose light is a pair of goggles it could take off. The tiny figure on its shoulder is the first passenger in the series.

A wolf-like creature with tall ears and glowing eyes bares its teeth in the dark, beside the words STILL BULLISH in orange. Number 100 in the series, and the artist gave it away: on May 23 it was minted free into the wallets of the board's builder, Austin Griffith, two other collectors named in the post, and fifty-nine more people who held the inks, among them Jamie Thingelstad. The wolf is a joke with teeth. Two weeks after the crash, the artist's answer to the question everyone on the board was asking was a snarl and the word STILL, sent to everyone who had stayed.

A skull mask fills a brown frame, its two eyes glowing yellow like headlamps, a beam falling from them to the lower right. Blue tubes rise from the top of the head, a crown of red zigzag runs under the cheekbone, and a necklace of white beads hangs across the jaw. The ground is a curtain of brown scribble. It is the last of the framed heads, and the one where the eyes and the beam are the same yellow as the paint. A skull with its lights on is the whole wing in one picture: the thing is dead and it is still looking.

Go back to the bear with its lights on, and then to the bear with its lights off. Everything in the drawing is the same except the eyes, and the whole mood of the creature changes with them. Lit, it is a lamp in the dark; dark, it is small and worried. The artist drew both on the same day, half an hour apart, in the week the market fell. That is what the room is about: a light somebody decided to keep on.

A drawn border, and inside it one head filling every corner. That is the formula of this room, and it is where the masks of the summer begin. Twenty-three works, two of them from the first winter and the rest from a single month, May 5 to June 3, 2022, the month in which the artist noticed the count of inks had passed five hundred and the market fell out from under everyone who was buying them.

The borders vary: a wavy white and red ribbon, a row of blue stones, a strip of brown, a thin pink line. What they hold is always the same kind of thing, a face made of parts. Eyes are targets, spirals, X marks or lit squares. Teeth come in rows, as blocks, bones or a grille. Between the parts, the square is filled with scribble until nothing is empty. The artist's bio line on every platform was born readymade to please the eye, and these heads are what that looks like when it is honest: a face assembled to be looked at, with the assembly left showing.

Follow the X. It arrives on the first work in December 2021 as a cross on a wheel, returns in May on a gold skull, and by the end of the room it is sitting in both eyes of nearly every mask. Two of the heads carry words, BULLISH and WAGMI, the slogans people on the board were typing at each other in the worst month of the year. The X in the eyes and the slogans on the forehead are the same mask from two sides.
Before the mask month there were two framed faces, five months apart. Together they set out the border and the staring eye.

A wavy ribbon of white, red and blue runs around the edge, and inside it a machine of a face is packed with marks: a target eye with a black X across it, pink petals with yellow crosses, a blue wheel with a zigzag rim, and a long mouth of red lines at the bottom. It is the first framed head in the collection, drawn on December 9, 2021, the second day of the series, and the X is already there, laid over the eye like a cancellation. Eight months later, on August 14, 2022, it was one of the first five works of the series the artist sent to Jamie Thingelstad as a gift, within hours of his buying the origin piece of the Faces. The border the artist drew in December became, in effect, the frame it was delivered in.
A red frame around a grey field, and a white face with two round staring eyes and a round open mouth, its hair a tangle of white strokes.

May 5 to 7, six works in three days. The border becomes a strip or a row of stones, and the faces turn to skulls, crowds and the first spiral eye. On May 6 the artist noticed, in passing, that there were already 552 inks and the five-hundred mark had gone by uncelebrated.
Behind a border of blue stones on the left and a row of orange tiles below, a purple face with two ringed eyes bares a double row of white teeth.

A gold skull with two red X marks for eyes, a row of grey teeth, and white lines crawling over it like cracks. Around it the ground is black and the border cream, with green and blue stones scattered through both. This is the X at its plainest: two strokes crossed over each eye, drawn in red so that nothing else on the skull competes with them. A skull already has no eyes. Crossing them out anyway is the gesture of someone who wants to be sure, and in the first week of May 2022, with the inks selling and the market about to turn, the artist drew it in gold.
A head in profile facing right, with one square eye glowing yellow and a spiral inside it, white bars and yellow fence posts along the left and bottom.
A crowd packed into the frame: a skull with crossed eyes at the lower left, a row of small faces up the right edge, and figures with spiky hair across the top.
One eye a red X, the other a blue spiral, a bone of a nose between them, and a mouth of white blocks, all packed with purple, yellow and orange pattern.
Mid May. The heads turn mechanical, with dials, grilles and lettering, and then on May 25 four masks arrive in one day. The two with words were drawn a week after the crash.
A machine face with a row of six round dials for teeth, each marked with an X, and a beam of light crossing it from the left.

Black and red scribble over a gold figure, the word BULLISH written twice in red, once at the top and once at the bottom, drawn on May 20, a week after the crash, and the second time the word is not louder, only more insistent.

A mask with one eye a red cross on a yellow target and the other a spiral in a box, a mouth of white teeth in a yellow frame, and a border of pink dots around the whole thing. Blue and magenta scribble fills every space between the parts. The cross is red and the X is gone, but it does the same job: it cancels the eye it sits on. One of four masks drawn on May 25, the day the small black creatures were going by next door at the rate of several an hour. Nothing about this one is quick. It is a mask built like a shrine.
Two gold cylinders for eyes, each with a red slot, above a grille of white bars and a tangle of orange, black and white scribble.
A mask with a red heart for one eye and a smaller heart for the other, a row of yellow beads under them, and blue tubes across the forehead.

A mask of grey bone teeth, two eyes ringed with scalloped lace, one a planet with a ring and the other a square with a small face inside it, and the letters W A G M I along the top: we are all going to make it, the board's prayer in the spring of 2022, written on a mask with bones for teeth.

The last week of May and the first days of June. The X now sits in both eyes, the scribble gets looser, and the room ends with two heads drawn in a single morning. The collector bought the one with the beads, number 124, on June 1, the day it was made.
A head wrapped in white line, its two eyes spirals, held inside a square of black and a border of pink scribbled with gold.
A yellow face with a red X in each boxed eye, a tube for a nose, and a fan of blue rays coming in from the lower right.

A big mask fills the frame to the edges: two eyes with X marks in red and blue boxes, a long mouth of white teeth in a red band, and a crown of red and orange spikes around the top. Pink zigzag runs along the cheeks and the chin. Where the skull of May 6 had a plain red X on gold, this mask puts the X inside a box, surrounds it with pattern, and makes it one part of many. It also puts a crown on it. The crowned head with the cancelled eyes is the figure the whole wing will arrive at in October, and here it is at the end of May, grinning with every tooth, three weeks after the market fell.
A dark head with one blue spiral eye and one yellow, lit by a beam from the right, and lilac lines crackling around it like electricity.

A mask of yellow, black and blue with a red X in a round eye on the left and a square eye of zigzags on the right, a row of blue beads around the edge; the collector bought it on June 1, 2022, a few hours after it was drawn, for twenty xDai.
A yellow cross in one eye, a red cross in the other, a mouth of grey bars in a red frame, and scribble in blue, orange and white over a dark ground.

A face painted in black, brown and grey, with small pale eyes, a red mouth drawn in a snarl, and lines of red running down the cheeks. Colored scribble in lilac, blue and yellow floats over it without covering it, and there is no border. The mask has become a face again, with a nose, lids and lips, and the X has gone from the eyes. It is the one work in the room with shadow, and the one with tears, if the red is tears. After a month of masks that grinned through everything, the series drew a face on June 3 that is simply in pain, and did not frame it.

Twenty-four minutes later, the same morning, a face in loose line: one eye a red target under a spiky lid, the other a yellow oval, a red mouth with white teeth, inside a thin pink frame, as if the painted face had been too much and the mask had to be put back on.

Look again at the X. On the first work it is one stroke across one eye in a crowd of other marks. On the gold skull it is two plain red lines. By the last week of May it is drawn in both eyes, boxed, colored and surrounded by pattern, under a crown. Then, on the painted face that ends the room, it is gone, and two small eyes look out instead, with red running down the cheeks. The mask month ends with a face that could not keep the mask on.

Everything in this room is made of line. Figures are outlines, crowds are tangles, and where a body has color it is scribbled in, not painted. Twenty-three works, beginning with the first drawing in the whole series on December 8, 2021, and ending with four from the start of June.
